summary: Defines EAP-NOOB, an authentication method for setting up Internet-of-Things devices that ship with no pre-installed credentials. The device and server exchange keys over the network, and a short message carried out-of-band, such as a displayed code or a blinking light, lets the user confirm the exchange was not tampered with. The device needs some non-network way to show or receive that message. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When you pair a new gadget, you check a short code on its screen to make sure you are talking to the right one. This makes sure nobody sneaky slips in between.

questions: how to onboard iot devices without credentials
how does out of band authentication work in eap
what is the eap-noob oob step
subtitle: How a gadget with no credentials joins a network: swap keys over the air, then confirm them with a one-way message a person carries.

tldr.problem: Off-the-shelf IoT devices have no pre-installed credentials, no prior relationship with a server or user, and often only a one-directional interface such as a display, camera or blinking light. Registration, ownership and network credentials must all be set up at deployment.
tldr.mechanism: The device and server run an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange over the insecure network. A single user-assisted out-of-band message, in either direction, carries a secret nonce and a fingerprint that authenticate the exchange. After one successful Completion Exchange, a stored association supports fast reconnects without involving the user again.
tldr.outcome: It is an open, generic alternative to proprietary pairing methods for devices that have a non-network input or output of tens of bytes. It does not suit sensors with no user interface or devices the user cannot reach. It is a Standards Track document.

today: RFC 9140 is a Proposed Standard on the Standards Track, and it is updated by RFC 9965. It has not been obsoleted by any RFC.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Problem
sections.content:
RFC 9140 defines EAP-NOOB, a method for registration, authentication and key derivation for network-connected smart devices, such as consumer and enterprise appliances. These devices may be sold with no prior registration or credential provisioning, or may be recycled after a hard reset. So the registration in a server database, the ownership of the device and the credentials for network access and application security must all be established when the device is deployed.

The RFC lists the assumptions: no pre-established relation with the intended server or user, no pre-provisioned identifier or credentials, and an input or output interface that may allow only one-directional out-of-band (OOB) communication. Many proprietary OOB configuration methods exist; the goal here is an open standard and generic protocol.

The approach follows common pairing protocols. It performs a Diffie-Hellman key exchange over the insecure network and authenticates the established key with the OOB channel, which prevents impersonation. The security rests on the assumption that attackers cannot observe or modify messages on the OOB channel, and on the user having physical access to the device.

The OOB messages are dynamically generated. Static printed registration codes are not supported, because receipt of the OOB message authorizes the server to take ownership of the device, and a static code could leak and be misused later.
sections.eli5: A brand-new gadget does not know anybody yet. It shows a code, you carry the code to the server, and that proves the gadget really is the one in your hand.

sections.title: Protocol Overview and States
sections.content:
One EAP-NOOB run spans two or more EAP conversations, called Exchanges, because the user needs time to carry the OOB message between them. The Initial Exchange has four EAP request-response pairs. The server allocates an identifier, the sides negotiate a protocol version and cryptosuite, exchange nonces and do an ephemeral elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) key exchange. The OOB Step then follows, using one message in either direction.

While waiting, the peer may probe the server. If the OOB Step has happened, the probe leads to the Completion Exchange, which completes mutual authentication and key confirmation. If not, it leads to the Waiting Exchange. The Initial and Waiting Exchanges always end in EAP-Failure, and only the Completion Exchange can end in EAP-Success. Later, the Reconnect Exchange makes new keys, rekeys with ECDHE and updates algorithms without repeating the OOB Step.

Server and peer each keep a state from 0 to 4: Unregistered (0), Waiting for OOB (1), OOB Received (2), Reconnecting (3) and Registered (4). States 0 to 2 are ephemeral and 3 to 4 are persistent. The server MUST NOT repeat a successful OOB Step with the same peer unless the user explicitly resets the association or the server's persistent storage fails.

The peer starts with the generic Network Access Identifier noob@eap-noob.arpa. It tells the server that the peer expects EAP-NOOB and lets the AAA infrastructure route the session to the right server.
sections.eli5: Pairing takes a few visits. First the gadget and server say hello and make a secret. Then you carry a code between them. Then they check the code matches and remember each other for good.

sections.title: The Exchanges and the OOB Step
sections.content:
Every exchange begins with a common handshake: the identity request and response, then one EAP-NOOB pair (Type=1) in which the peer reports its identifier and state. The server then picks the exchange from the combination of server and peer states. Unregistered with an ephemeral state selects the Initial Exchange. OOB Received on either side, with the other side in state 1 or 2, selects the Completion Exchange. Both in Waiting for OOB selects the Waiting Exchange. Peer in Reconnecting with the server in Registered or Reconnecting selects the Reconnect Exchange. Other combinations need user action, and the server SHOULD report error 2002.

In the OOB Step the sender outputs the PeerId, a secret nonce Noob and a fingerprint Hoob, and the user delivers them to the other side. The receiver MUST compare the received Hoob with its own computed value. If they match it moves to OOB Received (2); otherwise it MUST reject the message. A sender may produce several OOB messages with different Noob values, and the RECOMMENDED lifetime, NoobTimeout, is 3600 seconds.

In the Completion Exchange the sides exchange message authentication codes, MACs and MACp, computed with keys derived in the key derivation step. If both verify, the exchange ends in EAP-Success and both move to Registered (4). If the OOB message expired or was spoofed, the recipient of an unrecognized NoobId reports error 2003. If OOB messages arrive in both directions at once, the server MUST behave as if only the server-to-peer message arrived.

In the Waiting Exchange the server may include SleepTime, a number of seconds the peer must wait before connecting again, to limit how often peers probe it.
sections.eli5: The server checks where each side is in the pairing steps and decides what to do next: start fresh, wait, or finish. Finishing needs the code you carried across.

sections.title: Message Fields and Encoding
sections.content:
In-band messages are JSON objects in UTF-8. Message types are integers 0 to 9, and a request and its response share the same type. Key fields include PeerId, PeerState, the version lists Vers and Verp, the cryptosuite fields Cryptosuites and Cryptosuitep, the direction fields Dirs and Dirp (1 for peer-to-server, 2 for server-to-peer, 3 for both), the public ECDHE keys PKs and PKp as JSON Web Keys, and the nonces Ns and Np, each 32 bytes.

ServerInfo and PeerInfo are application-specific JSON objects of at most 500 bytes. They can help the user match devices and deliver the OOB message, for example a brand, model and serial number. The RFC registers optional fields such as ServerName, ServerURL, PeerName, Manufacturer, SerialNumber, SSID and BSSID.

The secret Noob is 16 bytes. Hoob and NoobId are computed with the cryptosuite's hash function, truncated to the 16 leftmost bytes. The MACs use HMAC based on the same hash, truncated to the 32 leftmost bytes. The inputs are JSON arrays of 17 elements copied verbatim from the messages, with no re-ordering, re-encoding or added white space. Values sent as JSON strings, and nonces used as hash inputs, are base64url encoded without padding.

The RFC recommends that servers support both OOB directions (Dirs=3) but that a peer pick just one, because offering both can show the user two OOB messages when only one needs delivering.
sections.eli5: All the messages are written in a tidy label-and-value format, and the check codes are made by scrambling those exact words together, so changing even one letter would be noticed.

sections.title: Reconnecting, Rekeying and Keys
sections.content:
After a successful Completion Exchange, both sides store a persistent association with at least the PeerId, the negotiated version and cryptosuite, the NAI and a 32-byte shared key Kz. The peer also keeps the previous cryptosuite and Kz. When mobility, timeout or failure makes new session keys necessary, a side moves from Registered (4) to Reconnecting (3).

The Reconnect Exchange has three request-response pairs (Types 7, 8 and 9): negotiation, nonces with optional ECDHE keys, and MACs. The KeyingMode is 0 for the Completion Exchange and 1 to 3 for reconnects: 1 rekeys without ECDHE, 2 uses ECDHE with an unchanged cryptosuite, and 3 uses ECDHE with a new cryptosuite. Only modes 2 and 3 give forward secrecy. Neither side may accept a protocol version or cryptosuite it knows to be weaker than the current one.

Keys come from the one-step key derivation function in the NIST specification the RFC cites, with the hash taken from the negotiated cryptosuite. For the Completion Exchange the output bytes yield the EAP output keys MSK and EMSK (64 bytes each), a further application key AMSK, a MethodId, the MAC keys and Kz. The exported Session-Id is the Type-Code 0x38 (decimal 56) followed by the MethodId.

If the final response of a cryptosuite upgrade is lost, the peer can detect that the server still holds the old key and roll back, using the stored previous values. The server never rolls back.
sections.eli5: Once the two have met, they remember a shared secret. Next time they just prove they both know it, and they can swap it for a fresh one, without you having to carry another code.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
A problem is reported with an error notification message (Type=0) in place of the next request or response, after which the server MUST send EAP-Failure. The optional ErrorInfo text is at most 500 bytes. In the Initial Exchange, both sides return to Unregistered (0). In the Waiting and Completion Exchanges each side stays in its old state, except for the handling of error 2003. In the Reconnect Exchange both sides go to Reconnecting (3).

Error codes are grouped by thousands. The 1000s cover malformed input, such as an invalid NAI or ECDHE key. The 2000s cover peer and state issues: unwanted peer (2001), state mismatch needing user action (2002), unrecognized OOB message identifier (2003) and unexpected peer identifier (2004). The 3000s are negotiation failures with no common version, cryptosuite or direction. The 4000s is HMAC verification failure. The 5000s are application specific, and 6001 to 6999 are reserved for private and experimental use.

An OOB message with an unrecognized PeerId or wrong Hoob is not answered in-band. The receiver stays in Waiting for OOB (1) and should tell the user, since the message may have been delivered by mistake or by a malicious party. A bad MAC in the Completion Exchange does not change state, so a spoofed in-band message cannot force the user to repeat the OOB Step.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the gadget or server sends a numbered note saying what. For fake or wrong codes, they just quietly ignore them and wait for the real one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authentication rests on two features of the OOB message. The secret nonce Noob alone is enough to authenticate the key exchange, unless an attacker can eavesdrop on the OOB channel. The fingerprint Hoob lets the OOB receiver detect an impersonation on the in-band channel even if Noob leaks. The OOB sender is less protected, since the message goes one way; an attacker who learned Noob can pose as the receiver and make the association look complete only at the sender, which the user must resolve by resetting it. The RFC does not mandate an explicit confirmation to the sender.

The user has to identify the correct device. Mistakes between two new devices usually cause confusion rather than a security problem, and an opportunistic attacker gains nothing, because the OOB message is worthless to anyone who did not take part in the Initial Exchange. A supply-chain attack, a spoofed user interface or a misbinding attack (tricking the user into registering a different device) are not fully prevented. All protocols that rely on the user's physical access are exposed to misbinding. Server-side asset tracking against the PeerInfo and device certification can help.

The fingerprint and MACs cover the cryptosuite negotiation, which prevents downgrades, and both sides must refuse weaker suites. Direction negotiation cannot be protected the same way. For denial of service, the persistent association is never deleted by in-band messages, and the cap of 3600 seconds on SleepTime limits how long a spoofer can delay a device. The EAP security claims table lists confidentiality as not provided and mutual authentication, integrity, replay protection and fast reconnect as provided.

For privacy, PeerInfo and ServerInfo in a Reconnect Exchange are sent unencrypted, so they SHOULD be omitted unless critical data has changed. The PeerId is a unique identifier that could be used to track the peer during the association.
sections.eli5: A thief who only sees the gadget talking to the server cannot join in, because the secret is carried by you. The weak spot is you picking the wrong gadget by mistake, so be careful which one you hold.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned EAP Method Type 56 to EAP-NOOB and created a new registry of EAP-NOOB parameters with subregistries for cryptosuites, message types, error codes, ServerInfo fields and PeerInfo fields. New entries need Specification Required, except error codes 6001 to 6999, reserved for private and experimental use. The special-use domain eap-noob.arpa has also been registered.

Two cryptosuites are defined. Cryptosuite 1 uses the Curve25519 curve with SHA-256 and MUST be supported. Cryptosuite 2 uses NIST P-256 with SHA-256 and is RECOMMENDED. Each cryptosuite must name an ECDHE curve, a JSON Web Key encoding and a hash function whose output is at least 32 bytes.

The appendices cover the full state-transition tables, the application-specific parameters an application must define (such as OobRetries, recommended as 5 for channels with error detection or correction), roaming through an assigned NAI, and an example of encoding the OOB message as an https URL for a QR code or NFC tag.
sections.eli5: The registries are official lists, so everyone uses the same numbers and names for the same things.
